name: Information Asymmetry
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Gap Between Who Knows and Who Decides
lesson.summary: Explores how the vast difference in technical understanding between quantum computing insiders and outsiders creates a structural bias that shapes what gets believed, funded, and reported.
lesson.body:
You already know that cognitive biases distort judgment inside a single mind, but information asymmetry works differently: it's a bias that emerges *between* people, born from an unequal split in who actually understands what's going on. On one side sit the physicists, engineers, and executives who build and run quantum hardware. On the other sit investors, journalists, policymakers, and the general public, who must make decisions about funding, regulation, or simple belief without the years of training needed to independently check the claims being made. Because quantum mechanics genuinely resists intuitive understanding ,  superposition and entanglement don't map onto anything in ordinary experience ,  the gap between these two groups is unusually wide, and unusually hard to close by just "reading more."

This gap matters because it changes who gets to control the story. When an outsider can independently verify a claim, exaggeration gets caught quickly. But when only a small circle of specialists can evaluate whether a result is meaningful, the people making the claim also get to choose how it's framed, which comparisons are offered, and which caveats are left out. This isn't necessarily deliberate deception ,  the same asymmetry lets an insider unconsciously present the most flattering interpretation of ambiguous data, simply because no one outside the room is positioned to push back. The bias lives in the structure of the situation, not necessarily in anyone's intent.

Picture a hypothetical case to see the mechanism clearly. Suppose a company announces that its new processor has reached a milestone in "quantum performance" and reports a large improvement over its previous machine. To a specialist, evaluating that claim means asking pointed questions: was the comparison made on a task where quantum hardware has a genuine physical advantage, or a task chosen because it happens to flatter this particular machine? Did the reported improvement account for error rates, or only for raw qubit count, which by itself says very little about whether a computation can be trusted? An outsider reading a press release typically has no way to ask these questions, let alone answer them, so the headline number simply gets absorbed as reported. The specialist and the non-specialist are handed the same sentence, but only one of them can tell whether it means anything.

The consequence is a systematic skew rather than a random error. Random errors cancel out on average ,  some people overestimate progress, others underestimate it, and the noise washes out. Information asymmetry doesn't wash out, because it pushes in one direction: toward whatever framing benefits the party that already holds the technical advantage, whether that's attracting investment, winning a policy debate, or maintaining public confidence. Over time, this can inflate expectations well beyond what the underlying physics supports, since the group best equipped to correct the record is often the same group with the least incentive to do so.

Recognizing this bias doesn't require you to become a physicist yourself. It requires noticing when a claim depends entirely on trusting the claimant's expertise, and treating that dependency itself as useful information ,  a signal to seek independent replication, ask what's being compared to what, and be wary of any framing that only the insiders are equipped to question.
